record.title: AgentHorizon tests whether judges catch constraint violations in computer-use agents
record.summary: AgentHorizon is a benchmark for judging whether long-horizon computer-use agents followed precise user instructions, including paired near-miss failures where a trajectory completes the main task but violates a constraint. The authors report 1,373 instruction–trajectory pairs across three operating systems and six domains. GPT-5.5 through Codex reached 80.9 balanced accuracy on a difficult 528-task subset, but tooling effects varied across judges and exact recall for GPT-5.5 on bad side effects was 24.1%. Results are author-reported, and the English-only benchmark does not establish general reliability or production safety.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper and linked artifacts define AgentHorizon, a benchmark of 1,373 instruction–trajectory pairs (523 positive and 850 negative) spanning 166 hours, three operating systems and six domains. This establishes the benchmark artifact's reported scope, not its external validity.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a difficult 528-task subset, the authors report 80.9 balanced accuracy for GPT-5.5 used through Codex. This is a paper-reported result on the benchmark and has not been independently reproduced.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports inconsistent effects from agentic tooling across tested judges and configurations; GPT-5.5 direct prompting scored 68.6 balanced accuracy versus 80.9 through Codex, while Qwen 27B direct prompting scored 77.6 versus 70.4 through OpenCode.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For GPT-5.5, the paper reports 24.1% exact recall on the benchmark's bad-side-effect category, indicating that a judge can miss an unrequested harmful action even when the task outcome appears successful.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the 523 released positives were retained after review: two assessments agreed directly on 388 of 850 candidate positives, and arbitration retained 135 of the remaining 462 while excluding 327. They report no population inter-annotator agreement; a three-reviewer diagnostic covered 23 of 425 pairs, and cross-pass negative-label stability was Cohen’s kappa 0.802 over 850 negatives. A model-based residual-QA sample flagged an estimated 11.5% of tasks (18/156; Wilson 95% interval 7.4%–17.5%), not a human-validated error rate.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the benchmark scoring or reported judge results was performed; reported accuracy is not independently validated.

The authors report review and QA procedures but no population inter-annotator agreement; a diagnostic covered 23 of 425 pairs, cross-pass negative-label stability is not independent human agreement, and model-based residual QA estimated 18/156 flagged items (11.5%). Generalization to unseen applications, languages, operating systems and broad failures such as crashes or loops is unestablished.

brief.importance_rationale: If reliable, benchmarked trajectory judges could improve evaluation of long-horizon computer-use agents and expose harmful side effects hidden by apparently successful task completion. This paper contributes a bounded near-miss benchmark; results are author-reported, single-benchmark and do not establish production safety or general judge reliability.
limitations: Empirical judge results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced.
The benchmark emphasizes paired near-miss instruction violations and does not cover broad failure modes such as crashes or infinite loops.
The paper does not report an independent audit of annotator agreement; prior pilot exposure may weaken claims about an unseen test set.
Coverage is English-only and limited to the included applications, operating systems and task domains; screenshots and action logs do not capture every aspect of application state.
A high benchmark score is not a safety certification or evidence that a judge is suitable for production deployment.

Author documentation reports no population inter-annotator agreement. Its three-reviewer diagnostic covered 23 of 425 pairs; cross-pass kappa of 0.802 for negative labels is a different reliability measure. Model-based residual QA estimated 18/156 flagged tasks (11.5%; Wilson 95% interval 7.4%–17.5%), not a human-validated error rate.

The authors report 1,373 instruction–trajectory pairs across three operating systems and six domains. GPT-5.5 through Codex reached 80.9 balanced accuracy on a difficult 528-task subset, but tooling effects varied across judges and exact recall for GPT-5.5 on bad side effects was 24.1%. technical.claimed_result: The paper reports a benchmark for testing whether agentic judges detect precise constraint violations in long-horizon computer-use trajectories. The reported results show that judge performance varies by model and harness, while side-effect detection remains weak in at least one reported configuration.
technical.compute_or_cost: The benchmark contains trajectories totaling 166 hours. No complete inference-cost comparison or independent cost audit was performed in this review.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors report 80.9 balanced accuracy for GPT-5.5 through Codex on a difficult 528-task subset, compared with 68.6 for direct prompting; Qwen 27B scored 77.6 directly and 70.4 through OpenCode. GPT-5.5 exact recall for bad side effects was 24.1%. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced findings.
technical.implementation_status: The authors provide a public evaluation harness and dataset. Their landing pages were inspected, but the code and data were not downloaded or executed.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark pairs an instruction with a related task trajectory to create a near-miss negative: the agent may complete the main task while violating a specific user constraint. A judge must evaluate trajectory adherence and side effects, rather than endpoint completion alone.
technical.novelty: The benchmark focuses on long-horizon, fine-grained instruction adherence and near-miss violations, including unrequested side effects that can be hidden by successful task completion.
technical.regime: 1,373 instruction–trajectory pairs (523 positive, 850 negative), covering 166 hours, three operating systems and six domains. The difficult subset used for the highlighted GPT-5.5 result contains 528 tasks. The paper's benchmark is English-only and finite in application and task coverage.
technical.reproducibility: Public author code and data are linked, but no independent reproduction was performed. Annotation agreement and external validity remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares direct model prompting and agentic harness configurations, reporting inconsistent effects across GPT-5.5 and Qwen 27B. This comparison does not isolate all harness confounds or establish a general benefit from tool use.

brief.title: AgentHorizon tests whether judges catch constraint violations in computer-use agents
brief.why_it_matters: An agent can appear to finish a task while violating a precise user constraint or taking an unrequested action. AgentHorizon makes those near-miss cases measurable, while its reported low side-effect recall shows why task success alone cannot establish safe or faithful behavior.
